You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Patient: male | Age: None
Primary Diagnosis: Sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis
  Secondary: Spontaneous pneumothorax (right side)
  Secondary: Lung collapse
  Secondary: Surgical wound infection (Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii)
  Secondary: Hypovolemic shock due to surgical bleeding
  Secondary: Cardiopulmonary arrest
Symptoms at admission: Persistent dry cough for 4 weeks; Night sweats; Fever (unmeasured); Dyspnea (shortness of breath); Sudden pain in right chest radiating to neck; Weight loss of 8 kg
Anomalies/Findings:
  [ABNORMAL] Sputum Bacilloscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen) = Positive: 10 to 99 bacilli in 100 fields (normal: Negative (0 bacilli))
  [NORMAL] Procalcitonin = 0.09 (normal: < 0.5 ng/mL (varies by lab, but low indicates resolved infection))
  [CRITICAL] Respiratory Auscultation = Abolished breath sounds in right hemithorax (normal: Normal breath sounds in both lungs)
  [NORMAL] Oxygen Saturation = 98% (normal: 95-100%)
  [NORMAL] Heart Rate = 85 beats per minute (normal: 60-100 beats per minute)
  [BORDERLINE] General Condition = Pale 1/4 (normal: Normal skin color)
Procedures performed:
  • Right chest drainage on 03/02/2020
  • Pleurostomy on 03/03/2020
  • Closure of pleurostomy on 03/03/2020
  • Heimlich valve placement on 10/03/2020
  • Removal of Heimlich valve on 27/03/2020
  • New pleurotomy on 31/03/2020
  • Emergency exploratory thoracotomy on 07/04/2020
  • Packing of cavity with compresses on 07/04/2020
  • Right pneumonectomy by lateral thoracotomy on 11/04/2020
  • Tracheostomy on 11/04/2020
  • Removal of chest drain and Tracheostomy on 06/06/2020
Medications:
  • RI (Rifampin/Isoniazid) — Medicines to kill the TB bacteria. | Dosage: Continued treatment
  • Vancomycin — Strong antibiotic to fight the wound infection. | Dosage: Suspended on 02/04/2020
  • Meropenem — Strong antibiotic to fight the wound infection. | Dosage: Suspended on 02/04/2020
  • Amikacin — Antibiotic to fight the wound infection. | Dosage: Suspended on 02/04/2020
  • Oral Iron — Supplement to help make blood and fix anemia (pallor). | Dosage: Continued
Warning signs to mention:
  ⚠ Any new or worsening shortness of breath
  ⚠ Chest pain
  ⚠ Fever
  ⚠ Signs of infection at the wound site
  ⚠ Any concerns regarding the condition
Follow-up appointment: Follow-up appointment at [organization] and with the thoracic surgery team (date not specified, exams requested for this visit)
Ongoing treatment: TB medication (RI)
Ongoing treatment: Oral iron replacement
Hospital stay duration: 03 m 06 d 07 h
Outcome: alive
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
Your main diagnosis is Sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis (TB in the lungs), which was first diagnosed in 2019. You also developed several serious complications related to this TB. These include a spontaneous pneumothorax (air leaking into the space around the right lung), lung collapse, a surgical wound infection caused by a tough bacteria called Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, hypovolemic shock (a dangerous drop in blood volume due to bleeding from the surgical site), and a cardiopulmonary arrest (a temporary stop of the heart and breathing) that occurred on 10/04 due to low oxygen levels.

When you were admitted, you had been suffering from a persistent dry cough for 4 weeks, night sweats, and a fever that was not measured. You also experienced shortness of breath (dyspnea) and, one day before admission, sudden pain in your right chest that spread to your neck, along with worsening breathlessness. You had also lost about 8 kg in weight over the previous month. Your general condition was noted as pale 1/4 (mildly pale, which is not the normal skin color), but you were hydrated and conscious. Your heart rate was 85 beats per minute, which is within the normal range of 60 to 100 beats per minute. Your oxygen saturation was 98%, which is within the normal range of 95-100%. However, your respiratory exam showed abolished breath sounds in the right hemithorax (no air movement heard in the right lung), whereas normal breath sounds should be heard in both lungs. A sputum test called Bacilloscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen) came back positive, showing 10 to 99 TB bacteria in 100 fields, while a normal result would be negative (0 bacilli). A blood test called Procalcitonin was 0.09, which is within the normal range of less than 0.5 ng/mL, indicating that the infection was resolving.

You underwent several procedures during your stay. First, a right chest drainage was placed on 03/02/2020 to remove air or fluid. Then, a pleurostomy (a small opening in the chest wall to drain the lung space) was done on 03/03/2020 and closed on the same day. A Heimlich valve (a one-way valve attached to the drain to let air out but not in) was placed on 10/03/2020 and removed on 27/03/2020. A new pleurotomy (another chest opening) was performed on 31/03/2020. On 07/04/2020, you had an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (a major surgery to open the chest) because of significant bleeding from the TB cavities. The cavity was packed with compresses (gauze pads) to stop the bleeding. On 11/04/2020, you had a right pneumonectomy by lateral thoracotomy (surgical removal of the right lung) and a tracheostomy (a small opening in the windpipe to help with breathing). The chest drain and tracheostomy were removed on 06/06/2020.

For your wound infection, you were treated with strong antibiotics: Vancomycin, Meropenem, and Amikacin. These were suspended (stopped) on 02/04/2020 after your condition improved. You are continuing treatment with RI (Rifampin/Isoniazid), which are medicines to kill the TB bacteria. You are also taking Oral Iron, a supplement to help make blood and fix anemia (pallor).

Your hospital stay lasted 03 m 06 d 07 h. You are currently alive and in good general condition with no complaints. You must continue your TB medication (RI) and oral iron replacement. You have a follow-up appointment at [organization] and with the thoracic surgery team; the date is not specified, but exams have been requested for this visit. Please watch for warning signs such as any new or worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, fever, or signs of infection at the wound site. If you have any concerns regarding your condition, please call immediately.
